name: Tinder fungus (amadou, hoof fungus)
habitat: A hard bracket on dead and dying broadleaf trees — birch above all, also beech, maple and poplar. Boreal and temperate forest.
parts: inner flesh (the trama, worked into amadou)
identify: A hard, hoof-shaped or humped bracket fixed flat to the trunk, grey to grey-brown, 5-25 cm across.
Concentric ridges and furrows banding the upper surface like growth rings on a hoof.
The underside is a flat pore surface — fine pinholes, not gills.
Cut it open: under the hard crust is a suede-like tan-brown layer. That layer is the amadou, and it is why the fungus is worth carrying.
Woody and unyielding. It does not squash.

lookalikes.name: Artist's conk
lookalikes.danger: Low — not toxic, but it makes poor amadou and poor tinder, so mistaking it wastes the effort.
lookalikes.tell: Artist's conk has a flat white pore surface that BRUISES BROWN when you scratch it (which is what it is named for); Fomes does not mark that way, and it is hoof-humped rather than flat-shelfed.

lookalikes.name: Red-belted conk
lookalikes.danger: Low, but it is a conifer species with a different structure and it will not process into amadou.
lookalikes.tell: A distinct red-orange to red-brown BAND at the growing margin, and a sticky, resinous crust that melts under a flame. Grows mostly on conifers; Fomes is on birch and hardwood.

lookalikes.name: Birch polypore
lookalikes.danger: Low — it is also useful, as a plaster and a strop, but it is not this.
lookalikes.tell: Soft, pale, kidney-shaped with a smooth rolled edge and a fine white pore surface. It gives to a thumb; Fomes is stone-hard.

preparations.method: Cut away the hard crust and the tough pore layer, keep the suede-brown trama, slice it thin, and pound it until it is soft and felted. Traditionally then soaked in wood-ash lye or urine, dried, and pounded again.
preparations.for_use: A styptic pad pressed onto a bleeding wound — it is absorbent and clings, and this is exactly what it was sold to dentists and barber-surgeons for. The SAME material is the classic spark-catching tinder and an ember bed for `fire-bank-and-carry`.

preparations.method: Shave or scrape the trama into fluff; it takes a spark from flint and steel directly.
preparations.for_use: Ignition — see `fire-flint-and-steel`. Otzi carried this with him five thousand years ago.

preparations.method: A dry lump smoulders slowly without flaming.

cautions: It is a DRESSING, not a treatment. It presses and absorbs; direct pressure is still what stops a serious bleed — see `bleeding-direct-pressure`.
Raw fungus off a trunk is not sterile. Dry it, and keep a cloth barrier between it and open tissue where you can.
Do not eat it — it is far too tough to be food and it is not used internally.
Cutting brackets off living trees damages them; take from dead standing birch.
The traditional lye or urine soak is for making it soft and quick to catch, not for making it clean.
evidence: Documented as both tinder and a wound styptic for millennia — carried by the Tyrolean iceman, and sold commercially as a surgical haemostat into the nineteenth century. Modern clinical evidence is essentially absent; the absorbency and adherence are the mechanism, not a pharmacology.
